exercises.title: Binary search, traced
exercises.task: Read Search. Run prints left, right and mid at each step, the way you traced your own first version, for a value in the middle, the first, the last, and one that is missing.

exercises.title: Write the loop
exercises.task: Fill the loop condition and the two moves. The rule to keep true: if the target is in the slice, it is between left and right, both included.
hints: Your first version used for right-left > 1: it stopped with two elements left, and never looked at them. The range [left, right] still holds one element when left == right.
It also used left = mid and right = mid. mid was already checked, so it can leave the range: without the +1/−1, the range can stop shrinking and the loop never ends.
for left <= right, then left = mid + 1 or right = mid - 1.

exercises.title: Find the first bad build, like git bisect
exercises.task: Builds 0 to n−1: the old ones are good, and from some build on they are all bad. isBad is slow (it runs the test suite), so find the first bad build with as few calls as possible: about log₂ n. Return n if no build is bad.
hints: This is binary search for a boundary, not for a value: the answer is the first position where the condition becomes true.
Keep the answer in [lo, hi) with lo = 0, hi = n. If isBad(mid), the first bad build is at mid or before: hi = mid. Otherwise it is after: lo = mid + 1.
Stop when lo == hi: that is the answer. Go's sort.Search(n, isBad) does exactly this, and it is fine to read its source, but write it yourself.
